clue.text: Mysterious writer of legendary stories has the chance to include much learned material

indicators.note: to include tells us one piece is placed within the other, here inside the word for having the chance

parts.note: if someone has the chance to do something, they may

indicators.note: much of something is most but not all of it, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: lore is a body of traditional learning

explanation.surface: An enigmatic author of legends gets an opportunity to pack in plenty of scholarship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'much' drops the final letter of the learned material. Thomas Malory, compiler of the Arthurian Morte d'Arthur, is a famously obscure figure, so 'Mysterious' is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Thomas Malory wrote Le Morte d'Arthur, the Arthurian legends, and little is certain about who he was.

clue.text: Russian who wrote poems and composed tales in the outskirts of Murom

indicators.note: in tells us the rearranged letters sit within the outer letters
the outskirts of a word are its first and last letters
composed means arranged anew, so the letters of the words around it are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Russian poet and storyteller writing near the town of Murom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'composed' rearranges AND TALES to ANDELSTA, which goes 'in' MM, the first and last letters of Murom.
explanation.definitionFit: Osip Mandelstam was a major Russian poet who died in Stalin's camps.

clue.text: An American writer, original in fiction

indicators.note: in tells us the first piece is placed within the second

parts.note: a lie is a fiction, an untruth
ur- is a prefix meaning original or primitive, as in Urtext

explanation.surface: An American author with a fresh take on the novel.
explanation.walkthrough: UR goes 'in' LIE. Alison Lurie won the Pulitzer Prize for the novel Foreign Affairs.
explanation.definitionFit: Alison Lurie was an American novelist and Pulitzer Prize winner.

clue.text: Piece by an artist who paints in an Indian novel

definitions.text: who paints in an Indian novel

parts.note: RA, Royal Academician, is the crossword's standard artist
a man is a piece in chess or draughts

explanation.surface: A work by a painter who appears in a novel from India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' puts MAN beside RA. Raman is the signboard painter in R. K. Narayan's novel The Painter of Signs.
explanation.definitionFit: R. K. Narayan's The Painter of Signs centres on Raman, a sign painter in Malgudi.

clue.text: One often spoken of as if female, a person who precedes a prioress in famous fiction

definitions.text: who precedes a prioress in famous fiction

parts.words: One often spoken of as if female
parts.note: sailors and others traditionally call a vessel 'she'
man is a general word for a person

explanation.surface: A figure usually called 'she' turns out to be someone who goes before a nun in a celebrated story.
explanation.walkthrough: In Chaucer's Canterbury Tales the Shipman's Tale is followed directly by the Prioress's Tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaucer's sailor pilgrim tells his tale immediately before the Prioress tells hers in the Canterbury Tales.

clue.text: Make acceptable fruit brownie, say, for a stand-in ruler

parts.note: to sugar something is to sweeten it and make it more palatable
a plum is a fruit
a brownie is a kind of household fairy in folklore

explanation.surface: Instructions to sweeten some fruit and a chocolate cake for a deputy monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brownie' suggests a cake, but here it is the folklore house-sprite. In The Nutcracker this character rules the Land of Sweets in the prince's absence.
explanation.definitionFit: In Tchaikovsky's ballet she reigns over the Kingdom of Sweets until the prince comes back.

clue.text: "Not in —, and not in Asia, was mankind born" (Robert Ardrey)

definitions.text: "Not in —, and not in Asia, was mankind born" (Robert Ardrey)

parts.words: "Not in —, and not in Asia, was mankind born" (Robert Ardrey)
parts.note: the opening line of Ardrey's African Genesis, with one word missing

explanation.surface: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from a writer on human origins.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Ardrey's African Genesis (1961) opens with this line, arguing humanity emerged from violent ancestors in Africa.
explanation.definitionFit: Ardrey argued humans were not born in a state of blamelessness, the missing word of his line.

clue.text: 12's foe, certainly embracing exploitation in a dynasty

indicators.note: in tells us the combination sits within the dynasty

parts.note: the Ming dynasty ruled China from 1368 to 1644

indicators.note: embracing means holding the next piece inside

parts.note: OK means certainly, all right
use, as in making use of, means exploitation

explanation.surface: An enemy of 12, definitely abusive, within a ruling family.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embracing' and 'in' nest the pieces one inside another. 12 is 12-across, the Christmas ballet whose hero fights this villain.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Nutcracker the hero battles the rodent ruler at the head of an army of mice.

clue.text: This organ sees, we hear

indicators.note: we hear tells us the word is said aloud, not written

parts.note: to see is to understand, to know

explanation.surface: This body part can see, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I see' means 'I understand', so 'sees' is KNOWS, which sounds the same as the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The smelling organ on the face.

clue.text: Dickens character transported men termed "Bully"

indicators.note: transported means carried off somewhere else, so these letters move into a new order

explanation.surface: A Dickens figure: deported men called bullies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transported' rearranges MEN TERMED BULLY. The surface hints at convicts transported to Australia, as in Great Expectations.
explanation.definitionFit: Bentley Drummle is Estella's brutish husband in Great Expectations.

clue.text: Kind of religious day in Germany's only good city in which to find

annotationWithheld.why: Kind of religious day in Germany's only good city in which to find: EMBER inside NUR + G gives the city, but 'in which to find' has no job and the clue looks cut short; no scan or search available
annotationWithheld.clue: Kind of religious day in Germany's only good city in which to find

clue.text: Maybe half our 20, or hardly any going with us in Germany

parts.note: no, as in 'no time at all', means hardly any
uns is the German word for us

explanation.surface: A remark about how many of our words are of one kind, or that barely any of them travel with us in Germany.
explanation.walkthrough: 20 is the answer to 20-across, a stock of words; perhaps half of any such stock are naming words.
explanation.definitionFit: Naming words make up a large share, perhaps half, of any language's word stock.

clue.text: Some game birds seen in the middle of the year

indicators.note: these letters are visible running across the centre of the phrase that follows

explanation.surface: A note that certain game birds appear around midsummer.
explanation.walkthrough: An eye (also nye or nide) is a collective term for a brood of pheasants.
explanation.definitionFit: A brood of pheasants is called an eye, an old collective noun for these game birds.

clue.text: Dancing show with poll, something often seen at Christmas

parts.note: poll and nut are both slang for the head
a Christmas cracker is a paper tube pulled apart at British Christmas dinners

explanation.surface: A dance performance plus an opinion survey, both festive fixtures.
explanation.walkthrough: A Christmas cracker is a festive paper tube that two people pull apart with a bang. Tchaikovsky's ballet is a Christmas staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Tchaikovsky's ballet is a danced stage work traditionally staged at Christmas.

clue.text: A detective story character with greater advantage

parts.note: better means superior, greater
an edge is an advantage

explanation.surface: A sleuthing tale's figure who is better placed.
explanation.walkthrough: Gabriel Betteredge is the steward who narrates part of Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone, often called the first English detective novel.
explanation.definitionFit: Gabriel Betteredge is the old house steward narrating in Wilkie Collins's The Moonstone.

clue.text: Contrarily, French walls surround an old English city

indicators.note: surround tells us the turned word goes around the next piece
contrarily asks us to take the next word the opposite way round

parts.note: murs is French for walls
an is the indefinite article, A

explanation.surface: Perversely, French ramparts encircle an ancient English town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contrarily' turns MURS into SRUM, and 'surround' places A inside it. Old Sarum is the ancient site of Salisbury.
explanation.definitionFit: Sarum is the old Latin-derived name for Salisbury, whose original hilltop settlement was Old Sarum.

clue.text: Old story with Lee stirring a Lord Mayor's daughter long ago

definitions.text: a Lord Mayor's daughter long ago

indicators.note: stirring means mixing up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An ancient tale with a man called Lee rousing a mayor's daughter of olden days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stirring' rearranges O + STORY + LEE. Rose Otley is the Lord Mayor's daughter in Dekker's 1599 comedy The Shoemaker's Holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: In Dekker's The Shoemaker's Holiday Rose is the daughter of Sir Roger Otley, Lord Mayor of London.

clue.text: Novelist relaxed during supper? That's about right

indicators.note: during tells us a piece is placed in the middle of the meal

parts.note: supper is a meal

indicators.note: about means going round the next piece

parts.note: easy means relaxed

explanation.surface: A writer takes it easy over supper and asks if that's correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the relaxed word round the letter for right, giving ERASY, and 'during' sets that within the supper. The question mark keeps the surface conversational.
explanation.definitionFit: Meera Syal is a British writer whose novels include Anita and Me.

clue.text: Rose, wild but flipping good English worker in a transport company

indicators.note: flipping means turning the next two letters over end to end
in tells us the worker sits inside the company

parts.note: a line is a shipping or bus company
an ant is the crossword's stock worker insect

explanation.surface: A wild rose, and a wonderful English employee in a haulage firm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' turns the two abbreviations round to EG. It also reads as a mild British intensifier, like 'jolly', which hides its job.
explanation.definitionFit: Eglantine is the sweetbriar, a wild rose of hedgerows.

clue.text: Smart dame dancing in a capital novel

indicators.note: dancing tells us the letters of the words next to it move about

explanation.surface: A stylish woman dances in a city book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dancing' rearranges SMART DAME. Ian McEwan's Booker-winning novel shares its name with the Dutch capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Ian McEwan's 1998 Booker winner is named after the capital of the Netherlands.

clue.text: These rowers are transported when entertained by Fred

indicators.note: when hosted inside the name that follows, the rowers become a word for carried, so removing that name leaves them

parts.note: goods that are transported are freighted
taken as written

explanation.surface: A rowing crew is carried along while a man called Fred plays host.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue works in reverse: put the rowing crew inside the name Fred and you get a word meaning 'transported'. Taking Fred back out leaves the crew.
explanation.definitionFit: A racing boat crewed by eight oarsmen is itself called an eight.

clue.text: "Words, words, words" — but not one that Shakespeare wrote

definitions.text: "Words, words, words" — but not one that Shakespeare wrote

parts.words: "Words, words, words" — but not one that Shakespeare wrote
parts.note: Hamlet's reply to Polonius suggests a stock of words, and the clue adds that the playwright never used this particular word

explanation.surface: Hamlet's famous line, with the joke that the poet never used this term.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet answers 'Words, words, words' when asked what he reads. The answer is a whole stock of words, and the word itself does not appear in Shakespeare.
explanation.definitionFit: A stock of words, the lexicon a person or language has.

clue.text: Kingsley novel, neglected as yet

indicators.note: neglected suggests things left in disorder, so the letters are muddled

explanation.surface: A Kingsley book has been ignored so far.
explanation.walkthrough: 'neglected' rearranges AS YET. 'Kingsley' suggests Kingsley Amis, but the book is Charles Kingsley's 1848 novel Yeast.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Kingsley's first novel, Yeast: A Problem, appeared in 1848.

clue.text: He's distinguished, certainly Italian, and royal

parts.note: si is Italian for yes, certainly
R is the abbreviation for royal, as in RN

explanation.surface: A man of note, and definitely Italian and regal.
explanation.definitionFit: A knighted man is titled with this honorific, a mark of distinction.

clue.text: Escaped slave, reported to be angry

indicators.note: reported tells us the word is heard spoken rather than seen written

parts.note: to seethe is to be inwardly furious

explanation.surface: A runaway slave, said to be furious.
explanation.walkthrough: Sethe is the heroine of Toni Morrison's Beloved, who fled slavery in Kentucky.
explanation.definitionFit: Sethe, in Toni Morrison's Beloved, fled from slavery with her children.

clue.text: Gibbons mimics a particular English style, primarily

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so we take the opening letter of each word

explanation.surface: A writer named Gibbons copies a distinctly English manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gibbons' looks like an author such as Stella Gibbons, but it is the animals; 'mimics' is a second definition, since to ape is to imitate.
explanation.definitionFit: Gibbons are small tailless primates, a kind of lesser ape.

clue.text: Gay show with cross-dressing title role, not performed in the writer's lifetime

definitions.text: Gay show with cross-dressing title role, not performed in the writer's lifetime

parts.words: Gay show with cross-dressing title role, not performed in the writer's lifetime
parts.note: John Gay wrote a ballad opera whose heroine disguises herself as a man; it was banned and only staged after his death

explanation.surface: A description of a camp show with a drag lead that never reached the stage while its author lived.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gay' is John Gay, author of The Beggar's Opera; its banned sequel was not staged until 1777, after his death.
explanation.definitionFit: John Gay's sequel to The Beggar's Opera is named after its heroine, who disguises herself as a man.

clue.text: An odd term, originally meaning "prepared to be stained"

indicators.note: originally signals that these letters are not in their original order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A strange word whose first sense was 'ready for dyeing'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'originally' rearranges AN ODD TERM. A mordant is a chemical that fixes dye in fabric.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth treated with a mordant, a dye-fixing chemical, is ready to take colour.

clue.text: Colour TV channel for adults only?

parts.note: Sky is a British satellite television broadcaster
blue describes risque or pornographic material

explanation.surface: A colour television channel restricted to grown-ups.
explanation.walkthrough: Sky is a British satellite TV broadcaster; 'blue' in British usage means smutty, as in blue films.
explanation.definitionFit: A light, clear shade like a cloudless daytime heaven.

clue.text: One Greek goddess or another consuming chicken

indicators.note: consuming means one piece swallows the other, holding it inside

parts.note: Ate is the Greek goddess of mischief and ruin
a hen is a female chicken

explanation.surface: A Greek goddess, or perhaps a different one, eating poultry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'consuming' puts the chicken inside the second goddess, whose name is also the past tense of eat, so the surface is a goddess eating poultry.
explanation.definitionFit: Athene, or Athena, is the Greek goddess of wisdom.
